name: Times Literary Supplement cryptic crossword No 1,140

solutions.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

clue.text: Parchment covering books in honour of Doctorow?

blocks.note: something done in someone's honour is done for them
the novelist E. L. Doctorow, reduced to his initials

explanation.surface: A vellum binding made as a tribute to the author of Ragtime.
explanation.walkthrough: The question mark flags that Doctorow stands only for his initials. A forel is an old word for a parchment slipcase or cover for a book.
explanation.definitionFit: The noun names a kind of vellum case or wrapper, historically used to protect a volume.

clue.text: “She has all the — and freedom of a flower” (Wilde’s character description of Lady Chiltern)

definitions.text: “She has all the — and freedom of a flower” (Wilde’s character description of Lady Chiltern)

blocks.clueFragment: “She has all the — and freedom of a flower”
blocks.note: surface reading: a woman praised in floral terms, with one quality left blank
setter's reading: the stage direction introducing Lady Chiltern in An Ideal Husband supplies the missing word

explanation.walkthrough: This is a quotation clue: the gap is filled from Oscar Wilde's An Ideal Husband, where Lady Chiltern is introduced in the stage directions.
explanation.definitionFit: A flower's sweet scent pairs naturally with its freedom, so the missing noun is the bloom's perfume or smell.

clue.text: Could he become thus when badgered?

definitions.text: Could he become thus when badgered?

blocks.clueFragment: Could he become thus when badgered?
blocks.note: surface reading: would a person turn irritable if pestered?
setter's reading: he is the Water Rat of The Wind in the Willows, friend of Badger, whose nickname is also the word for short-tempered

explanation.walkthrough: 'Badgered' means pestered, but it also hints at Badger, his friend in Kenneth Grahame's The Wind in the Willows; the character's name is the very mood he would be in.
explanation.definitionFit: In British speech the adjective means irritable or bad-tempered, which is how anyone harassed tends to become.

clue.text: Tabler announcing what a boil specialist might do?

indicators.note: announcing something is saying it out for others to hear, so the sound counts rather than the spelling

blocks.clueFragment: what a boil specialist might do
blocks.note: a doctor who treats boils would pierce many of them

explanation.surface: A dinner guest speaking up about what a skin doctor does all day.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Tabler' looks like a strange word, but it means a member of the Round Table, here its most famous knight.
explanation.definitionFit: Sir Lancelot is one of King Arthur's knights who sat at the Round Table, so he is a tabler.

clue.text: Self-penned work takes off after August

indicators.note: one thing coming after another is placed behind it in the line

blocks.note: august as an adjective means grand or venerable
to take off someone is to mimic them

explanation.surface: An autobiography that becomes a hit after the summer holidays.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Self-penned' suggests an autobiography, but Self is the novelist Will Self; 'after' simply places the mimicking word behind the grand one. The capital on August hides the adjective.
explanation.definitionFit: Great Apes is a 1997 satirical novel by Will Self in which humans and chimpanzees swap places.

clue.text: Orwellian leader in power play with a German professor

indicators.note: a leader goes in front, so only the opening letter is taken
one thing sitting in another is enclosed by it

blocks.note: the first letter of the author's adjective
a deity is a power, as in the powers above

explanation.surface: A dictator from Nineteen Eighty-Four taking part in a political drama with an academic from Germany.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Orwellian leader' sounds like Big Brother, but it is only the first letter of the word.
explanation.definitionFit: C. P. Taylor's 1981 drama of that title follows Halder, a German literature professor drawn step by step into Nazism.

clue.text: Post men on The Pequod, perhaps after rising tide

indicators.note: in a down clue, rising means reading upwards, so the letters come back to front

blocks.note: taken as written before being turned
OR, other ranks, is the military abbreviation for ordinary soldiers
the Pequod is Ahab's whaler in Moby-Dick, an example of a vessel

explanation.surface: Mail carried by the crew of Melville's whaler once the sea level rises.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Post' looks like mail but is a job; 'on' puts the men ahead of the vessel, and 'after' puts that pair behind the upturned tide.
explanation.definitionFit: A post is a position or job, and the role of running a newspaper or journal is one such position.

clue.text: Banville’s Booker winner’s half the title Murdoch’s was

indicators.note: keeping only half of something means throwing the remaining half away

blocks.note: Iris Murdoch's Booker winner of 1978 repeats its three-word phrase twice

explanation.surface: A literary comparison of two Irish-connected Booker winners and their titles.
explanation.walkthrough: Murdoch's novel is The Sea, The Sea, so half of its title is exactly the name of John Banville's 2005 winner.
explanation.definitionFit: John Banville won the Booker Prize in 2005 for his novel about a widowed art historian revisiting a seaside village.

clue.text: Favourite game with companion, a naked lion tamer

indicators.note: naked means stripped of its covering, so the outside letters are peeled away

blocks.note: a favourite is a pet, as in teacher's pet
RU is rugby union
CH is a Companion of Honour
the word with its first and last letters gone

explanation.surface: A circus act pairing a pet and a game with a hairless big-cat trainer.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Lion tamer' reads as one phrase, but the big cat belongs to the wordplay and the tamer is Shakespeare's.
explanation.definitionFit: In The Taming of the Shrew this suitor subdues the fiery Katherina, so he is the play's title tamer.

clue.text: Finch family member close to indigo in tail

indicators.note: the close of a word is its end, so only its final letter is wanted
to be in something is to be enclosed by it, so one piece goes inside another

blocks.note: the final letter of the colour
a scut is the short tail of a rabbit, hare or deer

explanation.surface: A songbird with a blue-black patch near its tail feathers.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Finch' suggests a bird, but it is the family in Harper Lee's To Kill a Mockingbird.
explanation.definitionFit: Jean Louise Finch, known by her nickname, is Atticus's daughter and the narrator of the novel.

clue.text: Merchant Ivory’s debut features new director

indicators.note: a debut is a first appearance, so only the opening letter is taken
a thing that features something has it inside, as a film features an actor

blocks.note: Antonio is Shakespeare's Merchant of Venice
N is the standard abbreviation for new
the opening letter of the name

explanation.surface: The first Merchant Ivory film introduces a fresh film-maker.
explanation.walkthrough: Merchant Ivory reads as the film company, but Merchant is the Shakespeare role and 'debut' takes the first letter of Ivory; the merchant and that letter together hold the new abbreviation.
explanation.definitionFit: Michelangelo Antonioni was the Italian film-maker behind L'Avventura and Blow-Up.

clue.text: Modest Romeo hiding poetic inspiration

indicators.note: something hiding keeps a thing concealed inside itself, so the letters sit within the words

blocks.note: runs across the end of the first word and start of the second

explanation.surface: A shy lover keeping quiet about the muse behind his verses.
explanation.walkthrough: Romeo is not the NATO letter R here; the two words are just the container for the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: The Italian borrowing means creative fire or enthusiasm, the burst of feeling that drives a poet.

clue.text: Hard to get into unusually merry McGonagall?

indicators.note: unusually means not in the normal way, so the letters leave their normal order
getting into something means going inside it

blocks.note: H is the pencil abbreviation for hard
the letters to be rearranged

explanation.surface: A Harry Potter teacher who is difficult to cheer up.
explanation.walkthrough: McGonagall here is not the Hogwarts professor but William McGonagall, the Scottish Victorian versifier famed as the worst poet in English.
explanation.definitionFit: The question mark admits he is only an example of a versifier, and a notoriously poor one.

clue.text: Hearts, perhaps, in a Shakespearean courtship

blocks.note: first meaning: the card suit whose symbol stands for romance
second meaning: an old word for wooing found in Shakespeare

explanation.walkthrough: Hearts is a suit of cards, and it is the one associated with romance; Shakespeare uses the compound for the act of wooing.
explanation.definitionFit: Wooing is the pursuit of romance, while the red card suit symbolises romance itself.

clue.text: Poet stashing gold key in LA suburb, then drug

indicators.note: to stash is to hide away inside, so one piece is tucked within another
then means next in sequence, so the last piece is added at the end

blocks.note: Au is the chemical symbol for gold
D is a musical key
Bel Air is a wealthy district of Los Angeles
E is slang for the drug ecstasy

explanation.surface: A writer hiding bullion and a key in a Los Angeles neighbourhood before taking narcotics.
explanation.walkthrough: The gold and the key go in just after the first letter of the suburb, and the drug letter is tacked on the end.
explanation.definitionFit: Charles Baudelaire was the nineteenth-century French author of Les Fleurs du mal, a major lyric versifier.

clue.text: Crime writer having a go in bombed Slough

indicators.note: something bombed is blown apart, so its letters land in a new order

blocks.note: three short words supplying the letters to rearrange
a slough is a bog or swamp

explanation.surface: A mystery novelist trying her hand in a wartime-blitzed Berkshire town, a nod to Betjeman's 'Come, friendly bombs, and fall on Slough'.
explanation.walkthrough: Slough is a town west of London, so it reads as the thing bombed; in fact the anagram signal works on the three words before it, and Slough is a wetland.
explanation.definitionFit: Dame Ngaio Marsh was a New Zealand author of detective novels starring Roderick Alleyn, one of the Golden Age queens of crime.

clue.text: As was Crichton, Breaking Bad and Mailer

indicators.note: breaking something smashes it into pieces that can be put back differently

blocks.note: taken as written
taken as written; Norman Mailer in the surface

explanation.surface: Michael Crichton listed alongside a TV drama and Norman Mailer.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Breaking Bad' reads as the television series, but the first word is the anagram signal and the second joins Mailer as fodder. Crichton is not the novelist but J. M. Barrie's butler.
explanation.definitionFit: J. M. Barrie's play The Admirable Crichton is named for its capable butler, so the adjective is what Crichton was.

clue.text: Border crossing husband goes over in Pullman briefly?

indicators.note: a road crossing a field runs across its middle, so one piece sits astride another
going over is turning right round, so the result is flipped end to end

blocks.note: a lip is a rim or edge
H is the abbreviation for husband

explanation.surface: At a frontier post, a husband travels across in a luxury railway carriage.
explanation.walkthrough: A Pullman is a luxury railway carriage, but here it is the novelist Philip Pullman, and 'briefly' shortens his first name.
explanation.definitionFit: Phil is the short form of Philip, the first name of the author of His Dark Materials.

clue.text: Unscrupulous beauty Miss America to open hospital

indicators.note: to open something is to split it apart and get inside

blocks.note: a miss is a young lady
US is the abbreviation for the United States
a san is a sanatorium, a hospital for convalescents

explanation.surface: A ruthless beauty queen, Miss America, is booked to cut the ribbon at a new hospital.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Miss America' reads as one beauty title, but Miss and America are separate pieces.
explanation.definitionFit: Jane Austen's short epistolary novel portrays a beautiful, manipulative widow who schemes without conscience.

clue.text: Lover of Carstone, a real cad in a bad way

indicators.note: something in a bad way is in disorder, so its letters are muddled

blocks.note: the letters to rearrange

explanation.surface: A woman's suitor turns out to be a genuine bounder who is down on his luck.
explanation.walkthrough: Carstone is Richard Carstone in Dickens's Bleak House, a ward in Jarndyce and Jarndyce; a cad is a dishonourable man.
explanation.definitionFit: In Bleak House Richard Carstone secretly marries his cousin, a fellow ward of John Jarndyce, who loves him faithfully.

clue.text: Madame Bovary’s contrary soul enthralling a French gentleman

indicators.note: contrary means going the opposite way, so the letters run backwards
to enthral originally meant to hold captive, so one piece is held inside another

blocks.note: âme is French for soul
M is the abbreviation for Monsieur

explanation.surface: Flaubert's heroine has a perverse spirit that captivates a Frenchman.
explanation.walkthrough: The soul is French, in keeping with the novel; the accent on âme is dropped.
explanation.definitionFit: Flaubert's heroine is christened Emma, and she becomes Madame Bovary on marrying Charles.

clue.text: McBain twist: jumper died a victim of strangulation

blocks.note: Ed McBain, author of the 87th Precinct crime novels
to wind is to twist or coil
a roo is a kangaroo, a jumping animal, not a sweater
D is the abbreviation for died

explanation.surface: The plot twist in a crime novel: a person in a sweater has been strangled.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Twist' reads as a plot twist in a thriller, and in British English a jumper is a sweater; both are misleads.
explanation.definitionFit: Dickens left The Mystery of Edwin Drood unfinished, and the young man is widely believed to have been throttled by his uncle John Jasper.

clue.text: Doctor Who’s content kept from TV guide?

indicators.note: the content of something is what lies inside it, so only its middle is taken
what is kept from something is withheld and not allowed in

blocks.note: the inside letter of the three-letter word
a listings guide tells you what's on

explanation.surface: Plot details of Doctor Who are withheld from the television listings.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Doctor Who' reads as the BBC series, but the first word is the definition. 'Content' means the inside of the next word, the only letter left once its ends go.
explanation.definitionFit: Dr John Watson is Sherlock Holmes's companion and chronicler, the most famous medical man in detective fiction.

clue.text: Agent backing revolutionary ultra writer against the Ancients?

indicators.note: backing means moving in reverse, so the letters run the other way
a revolutionary overturns the existing order, so these letters are rearranged

blocks.note: a rep is a sales representative, an agent for a firm
the letters to rearrange

explanation.surface: A spy supporting an extreme radical author who opposes the old order.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Revolutionary ultra writer' reads as one political extremist, but the first word is the anagram signal and only 'writer' belongs with the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Charles Perrault, collector of fairy tales, led the Moderns in the 17th-century French Quarrel of the Ancients and the Moderns.

clue.text: Romantic city gent not making a bride joyful?

definitions.text: gent not making a bride joyful?

blocks.note: first meaning: the French capital, famed as the city of love

blocks.clueFragment: gent not making a bride joyful?
blocks.note: second meaning: Juliet's unwanted suitor in Romeo and Juliet, of whom she says he shall not make her there a joyful bride

explanation.walkthrough: The second half echoes Juliet's line about the count her father wants her to marry: 'He shall not make me there a joyful bride.'
explanation.definitionFit: The same name belongs to the French capital, celebrated for romance, and to the young count Juliet refuses in Shakespeare's tragedy.

clue.text: One caught by warm gust, wings failing

definitions.text: One caught by warm gust, wings failing

indicators.note: by means beside, so one piece stands next to another
wings are the outer edges, and when they fail only the middle survives

blocks.note: the Roman numeral for one
C is the cricket scoring abbreviation for caught
the two inner letters of the word
the two inner letters of the word

explanation.surface: Someone swept up in a hot blast of air as his wings give way.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue is both definition and wordplay: the hot air near the sun melts the wax, and the boy's wings fail.
explanation.definitionFit: In Greek myth Daedalus's son flew too near the sun, the wax holding his feathers melted, and he fell into the sea.

clue.text: Genealogical book that a Rolling Stone can’t put down?

definitions.text: that a Rolling Stone can’t put down?

blocks.note: first meaning: Alex Haley's 1976 book tracing his family back to an African ancestor

blocks.clueFragment: that a Rolling Stone can’t put down?
blocks.note: second meaning: a rolling stone gathers no moss, and a wanderer never settles in one place

explanation.walkthrough: 'Can't put down' sounds like praise for a gripping read, but it means a rover can never settle; a Rolling Stone is also a member of the band, hence the capitals.
explanation.definitionFit: Haley's family history is the famous title, and to put down this noun is an idiom for settling somewhere permanently.

clue.text: Gently does it at first with a vacuous remark

indicators.note: at first means at the start, so only the opening letters are taken
something vacuous is empty, so the inside is cleared out and only the shell remains

blocks.note: the opening letter
the opening letter
the word with its middle emptied

explanation.surface: 'Gently does it' is a warning to go carefully, followed here by a pointless comment.
explanation.walkthrough: The familiar phrase 'gently does it' hides the definition: the first word alone is the surname of Douglas Adams's detective.
explanation.definitionFit: Dirk Gently is the holistic detective in Douglas Adams's novels, so his forename completes the surname.

clue.text: A problem this Scottish cop has when writing his name?

definitions.text: A problem this Scottish cop has when writing his name?

blocks.clueFragment: A problem this Scottish cop has when writing his name?
blocks.note: surface reading: a Scottish policeman struggles to spell his own name
setter's reading: Ian Rankin's Edinburgh inspector shares his surname with a picture puzzle, so writing it out that way would make one

explanation.walkthrough: Ian Rankin's detective inspector shares his surname with a puzzle in which pictures and letters spell out a word, so his name could itself be written as one.
explanation.definitionFit: The word means both a riddle made of pictures and symbols and the surname of Rankin's Edinburgh detective.

clue.text: “— are a slavish herd and fools in my opinion” (Jean de la Fontaine)

definitions.text: “— are a slavish herd and fools in my opinion” (Jean de la Fontaine)

blocks.clueFragment: “— are a slavish herd and fools in my opinion”
blocks.note: surface reading: a scornful verdict on some group who follow blindly
setter's reading: the French fabulist's line supplies the missing plural noun

explanation.walkthrough: This is a quotation clue: the gap is filled from Jean de La Fontaine, the seventeenth-century French writer of fables, scorning those who only copy others.
explanation.definitionFit: A slavish herd follows rather than invents, which describes copycats who reproduce the work of others.

clue.text: “A sad soul can kill you quicker, far quicker, than a germ” (John —)

definitions.text: “A sad soul can kill you quicker, far quicker, than a germ” (John —)

blocks.clueFragment: “A sad soul can kill you quicker, far quicker, than a germ”
blocks.note: surface reading: a warning that despair is deadlier than disease
setter's reading: the gap asks for the surname of the American novelist who wrote the line, in Travels with Charley

explanation.walkthrough: This is a quotation clue in reverse: the words are given and the author's surname is missing. The line comes from Travels with Charley.
explanation.definitionFit: The author of The Grapes of Wrath and Of Mice and Men wrote this remark about melancholy in his travel memoir.

clue.text: Western writer Eastern journos deny embracing

indicators.note: to embrace is to hold within, so the letters lie inside the words
starting from the eastern end of an across line means reading right to left

blocks.note: runs across the end of the first word and start of the second

explanation.surface: Reporters in the East refuse to cover a cowboy novelist.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Western' and 'Eastern' look like a matched pair, but the first is part of the definition and the second tells you to read from the right.
explanation.definitionFit: J. T. Edson was a prolific English author of cowboy novels such as the Floating Outfit series.
